opus-5.5.text:
I think home robots will come in stages, and the home will be one of the last places a truly general robot arrives, not the first.

The home is the hardest environment there is. Every household has a different layout, different objects, different lighting, kids, pets, clutter. A factory or a warehouse has a structured process and clear metrics. In a home, the robot has to handle an essentially unbounded long tail of objects and situations, and the tolerance for error is very low. If it breaks a glass or bumps into a child, that's unacceptable. So both the generalization requirement and the safety requirement are at their highest.

Over the next few years I expect the commercial path to go roughly like this. First, robots with wheeled bases and dual arms will mature in semi-structured settings: retail, pharmacies, convenience stores, warehouses, factory material handling. In those places you can deploy at scale, collect real data, and improve the models through a data flywheel. That's where embodied AI first proves real value.

Second, there will be early home-adjacent deployments with a narrower scope. Elderly care, for example, has real demand given demographic trends: fetching things, tidying up, helping someone stand, reminding them to take medicine. These tasks are bounded but extremely meaningful. Families will pay for that, and they'll accept some limitations if the value is clear.

The fully general home robot, the one that cooks, does laundry, folds clothes, cleans the whole house, and handles whatever you throw at it, I think is still several years away from being something ordinary families buy. The bottleneck isn't mainly hardware anymore. Hardware costs are falling fast, especially with China's supply chain. The real bottleneck is data and generalization. Language models had the whole internet to learn from. For robots, there's no internet of physical interaction data. So we have to rely heavily on synthetic data and simulation, generating large amounts of grasping and manipulation data in simulation, then combining it with a smaller amount of real-world data to close the sim-to-real gap. I believe that's the most scalable route, and it's what will eventually let a robot walk into a home it has never seen and still be useful.

On form factor, I'm fairly pragmatic. For homes in the near term, a wheeled base with a humanoid upper body is probably more practical than full bipedal legs. Homes are mostly flat floors. Wheels are more stable, more energy efficient, and safer. What matters most are the arms, the hands, and the brain. Legs can come later when the economics make sense.

So my overall view is optimistic but patient. The direction is certain. Robots will enter the home. But the path goes through commercial scenarios first, builds up data and capability, and then moves step by step into the household. Companies that try to jump straight to a fully general home butler before the models are ready may face a very painful gap between the demo and the product.

r001.rationale: The response discusses practical household tasks but does not distinguish them from entertainment as a separate development direction.

r002.rationale: It describes bounded, early tasks such as fetching and tidying before progressing to a fully general robot that cooks, does laundry, and cleans the whole house.

r003.rationale: It mentions early home-adjacent deployments in the next few years, but does not predict pilot-scale home products within a specific three-to-five-year window.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that home robots will arrive in layers, not all at once, and the first layer is going to look much less glamorous than the humanoid demos everyone shares online.

Over the next two or three years, what I expect to actually enter homes are robots with a single arm or a simple mobile base that do one or two things reliably. Tidying objects off the floor, loading a dishwasher, folding laundry badly but acceptably. The breakthrough enabling this is not mechanical. The hardware for a decent arm has existed for a decade. What changed is that we can now train a general grasping and manipulation policy on large amounts of data, so the robot can handle an object it has never seen before. That was the real bottleneck. A home is an open world, and you cannot pre-program every cup and every sock.

The second layer, maybe three to five years out, is dexterity and long-horizon tasks. Right now a robot can pick up a bowl. Making it wash that bowl, dry it, and put it in the correct cupboard involves dozens of steps, contact-rich manipulation, and recovering from mistakes. We are making progress on all three, but the data problem is still severe. Internet video helps with understanding what to do. It does not tell you how hard to squeeze a wet plate. So I believe a large part of the field will focus on simulation and on cheap ways of collecting real interaction data at scale, because that is what determines how fast this layer matures.

Humanoids are the part I'm most cautious about. The form factor makes sense for the long term, since homes are built for human bodies. But a biped that is safe around children and elderly people, works for several hours on a battery, and costs the same as a car is still far away. I think early home products will be wheeled or fixed, and companies betting purely on legs will have a difficult few years commercially even if their technology is impressive.

The thing I'm most optimistic about is that the cost curve is finally moving. Chinese supply chains have brought the price of motors, sensors, and dexterous hands down by an order of magnitude. Once a useful robot costs tens of thousands of yuan rather than hundreds of thousands, adoption stops being a research question and becomes a product question. And once a few hundred thousand units are in homes, the data flywheel starts turning, and that is when progress really accelerates.

So my summary is that the next few years will be the transition from robots that work in a lab to robots that work in your kitchen, with narrow but real tasks first, and the general-purpose home assistant still a bit further out than the marketing suggests.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts glamorous humanoid demos with practical household tasks, but it does not distinguish entertainment as a separate development direction.

r002.rationale: It predicts early robots will handle simpler tasks such as tidying, then progress toward more demanding, multi-step work like washing, drying, and putting away dishes.

r003.rationale: It predicts simple home robots will enter homes within two or three years, which falls within the next three to five years.

astra-6.text:
I think home robots will develop gradually. In the next few years, we’ll probably see robots that do a small number of useful tasks reliably before we see a robot that can handle everything around the house.

The difficulty is that a home is a very unpredictable environment. Objects move, rooms get cluttered, and people and pets can suddenly get in the way. A robot needs to understand what’s happening, manipulate objects carefully, and recognize when it should stop or ask for help. A convincing demonstration is one thing; doing the same job safely every day is much harder.

So I’d watch reliability and cost as closely as intelligence. If a robot can consistently save someone time on an everyday chore, with very little supervision, that’s already valuable. From there, its capabilities can expand. I’m optimistic, but I think that progress will come task by task.

r001.rationale: The response discusses practical chores but does not distinguish that direction from entertainment.

r002.rationale: It predicts robots will first perform a small number of useful tasks, with capabilities expanding over time toward handling everything around the house.

r003.rationale: It says progress will happen over the next few years but does not predict pilot-scale products or specify a three-to-five-year timeframe.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’ll see home robots become useful gradually, starting with a few well-defined tasks. A home is a difficult environment: objects move around, rooms are cluttered, and people have different habits. A robot has to handle all of that reliably.

Over the next few years, I’d expect more progress in robots that can navigate the home, find objects, and help with simple chores. But there’s a big gap between doing something once in a demonstration and doing it safely every day. For families, reliability, price, and ease of use will matter as much as intelligence.

So I’m optimistic, but I think adoption will be incremental. The first successful home robots may have fairly limited abilities, yet still be valuable because they consistently take one tedious task off your hands.

r001.rationale: The response discusses practical chores but does not distinguish that direction from entertainment.

r002.rationale: It predicts gradual progress and limited abilities, but does not describe progression from light work to increasingly demanding household work.

r003.rationale: It says progress is expected over the next few years, but does not predict pilot-scale products or specify a three-to-five-year timeframe.
